units.text: Begin in the owner account on the left. The S3 object is encrypted using the customer managed KMS key shown beneath the bucket.
The upper gate is S3 access. The bucket policy in Account A and identity permissions in Account B must authorize the intended object read.
The lower gate is KMS decryption. Follow the key policy in the owner account and the reader role permissions in the other account.
The reader role on the right participates in both checks. Permission to read an S3 object does not by itself authorize use of its KMS key.
The complete diagram has two gates, and both must allow the request. Explicit denies can still block access even when these individual permissions appear present.
Start at step one on the upper left. Create a pending credential and store that version with the pending staging label.
Follow step two on the right. The target service must be updated to recognize the pending credential; changing only the stored secret is insufficient.
Step three tests the pending credential against the target service. Verify that it works before promoting it for normal use.
At step four, promote the tested version to current. The previous version can be retained, while rollback still needs deliberate operational handling.
Follow the whole loop, then read the footer. Verify application retrieval and rollback behavior. Rotation must be configured, and plaintext credentials must stay out of logs.
Begin with Parameter Store on the left. Hierarchical names organize configuration values by application, environment, and other operational boundaries.
Its SecureString option encrypts sensitive configuration with KMS. That encryption does not automatically rotate the underlying credential.
The central question is what kind of value this is and how the application uses it. Configuration settings and managed credentials have different lifecycle needs.
On the right, Secrets Manager focuses on credentials and other secrets. Its rotation and replication capabilities still need service-specific configuration and testing.
With both choices visible, select the service by the required lifecycle. Keep encryption, retrieval permissions, rotation, and recovery as separate design decisions.
